title: What is the ILO, and why does it matter to Indian workers?
author: Editorial Desk
summary: A short guide to the International Labour Organization and its unusual three-party structure.
body:
The **International Labour Organization (ILO)** is the United Nations agency for the world of work. It was created in **1919**, as part of the Treaty of Versailles that ended the First World War, and India has been a member from the start. Its headquarters are in Geneva, Switzerland, and it now has 187 member States. For a union like BMS, whose leaders travel to Geneva every year, the ILO is a regular workplace. For an ordinary worker in India, it can seem remote. This post explains what the ILO is and why its work reaches the factory floor.

## A short history

The ILO was set up in 1919 on the idea that lasting peace depends on social justice, and that no country can improve working conditions alone if its competitors do not. If one country allows very long hours and very low wages, it can undersell others, and the pressure pushes everyone downwards. International standards are meant to stop that race to the bottom. The ILO is described on its website as the only tripartite United Nations agency, which sets it apart from the rest of the UN family.

## Tripartite by design

What makes the ILO different is that it is **tripartite**. Each member country sends a delegation with representatives of the government, of employers and of workers, and each of the three groups has its own voice. Workers' representatives are chosen in consultation with the most representative trade union organisations of that country. This is why the voice of an organisation like BMS is heard at Geneva.

The same idea is applied at home. India's government works with employer and worker organisations in the Indian Labour Conference and the Standing Labour Committee, which are national bodies for tripartite consultation. BMS's website says it sits on both, and on many other bipartite and tripartite bodies.

## How the ILO is organised

Three organs do the main work.

- **The International Labour Conference (ILC)** is the general assembly. It meets every year in June in Geneva and is the main policy-making body.
- **The Governing Body** is the executive council, which meets three times a year.
- **The International Labour Office** is the permanent secretariat that carries out the programme day to day.

## What it does

- **Sets international labour standards**, called Conventions and Recommendations, on subjects such as forced labour, child labour, equal remuneration, non-discrimination, safety at work and freedom of association. A Convention is legally binding on a country that ratifies it. A Recommendation is not ratified; it guides governments in making policy.
- **Supervises the application of standards.** At the Conference, a committee examines how member States implement the Conventions they have ratified. This is where governments, employers and workers question one another in public.
- **Provides technical assistance** to governments and social partners, helping them draft laws and build institutions.
- **Collects and publishes research and statistics** on employment and decent work.

## India and ILO standards

India is a founding member. A Government source records that India had ratified 43 Conventions and one protocol as of 2015. Among the eight "core" or fundamental Conventions, India had ratified six by 2017: the Forced Labour Convention (No. 29), the Abolition of Forced Labour Convention (No. 105), the Equal Remuneration Convention (No. 100), the Discrimination (Employment and Occupation) Convention (No. 111), the Minimum Age Convention (No. 138) and the Worst Forms of Child Labour Convention (No. 182). The two it had not ratified were Convention 87 on freedom of association and Convention 98 on the right to organise and collective bargaining. A press report of that time attributed this to restrictions on government employees under statutory rules, and noted that ratification is voluntary and has no fixed timeline.

These two Conventions are of direct interest to trade unions, and the question of whether and when to ratify them is one that unions and governments have discussed in tripartite settings. Readers who want the current position should check the ILO's NORMLEX database, since ratification status can change.

## The annual conference

Once a year, in June, member countries meet in Geneva for the International Labour Conference. For example, the 113th session was held from 3 to 14 June 2025 with over 4,000 delegates from the 187 member States. It adopted Convention No. 192 on biological hazards in the working environment, along with amendments to the Maritime Labour Convention. The Conference adopts standards, discusses reports and holds a plenary at which leaders of delegations speak. Much of the real work is done in committees, where each group negotiates the wording of texts line by line.

BMS has regularly sent delegations to the ILC, and its website says that it leads the Indian workers' delegation. At the 2025 session, BMS's organising secretary B. Surendran addressed the plenary on 6 June. According to a report in *Organiser*, he urged the ILO to take up the international portability of social security and global parameters for skill certification, raised the situation of migrant workers and of gig and platform workers, and called for frameworks to prevent job loss caused by artificial intelligence. A BMS report on the session lists BMS members leading or serving in committees on standards, the platform economy, the transition from informal to formal work and protection from biological hazards. These are reports from the organisation and a friendly publication, and the ILO's own records of the proceedings are the best place to check exact wording.

## Why it matters at home

Many Indian labour laws, from minimum wages to the prohibition of child labour, are influenced by ILO standards. The Constitution's own language on equal pay and on protecting children, discussed in an earlier post, parallels ILO Conventions on the same subjects. When the Government of India, trade unions and employers sit together at Geneva, they negotiate positions that affect every worker back home: how platform work should be regulated, how social security can follow a migrant across borders, and how safety standards are set.

For a worker, the practical lesson is that a protection which seems purely national often has an international root, and that an organisation which takes part in ILO debates can bring that experience back to bargaining at home.

## What to watch

Two questions will matter in the coming years: how countries respond to the new Convention on biological hazards, and whether India moves on the freedom-of-association Conventions. BMS's declared approach is to appreciate good initiatives of Government and to oppose measures that harm labour, and it will apply that approach in Geneva as it does in India.

The next posts in this series will follow BMS delegations to Geneva, year by year.
